title: E-bike 'hoon boys' not saddled with insurance
full_text:
E-bike riders will not be forced to take out insurance in NSW despite research showing the number of cycling crashes has soared along with use of the devices, which sometimes travel at motorcycle speeds and now account for 40 per cent of smashes.
The Minns government says it will accept the recommendation of a state productivity commission report that the cost of a compulsory insurance scheme for e-bikes would punish legitimate users for the illegal behaviour of a minority of "Hoon Boy Harrys".
The NSW Productivity and Equality Commission says a compulsory insurance scheme could cost $470 million to $1 billion, mainly due to deterred trips and increased costs for other transport. It recommends enforcement of existing laws instead.
Commissioner Peter Achterstraat blamed "a small number of Hoon Boy Harrys [behaving] recklessly [who] selfishly put the enjoyment of other people at risk" for the growing community backlash against devices such as e-bikes and e-scooters.
Under current rules, e-bikes in NSW are allowed to have up to 500 watts of power, with that set to be slashed to 250 watts from 2029. Although e-bikes' acceleration is supposed to cut out at 25km/h, widespread use of devices capable of higher speeds, illegal on public roads, has left many pedestrians and other road users fearful they are as powerful as motorcycles.
Use of e-mobility devices has exploded, with trips taken on e-bikes through shared schemes rising from 256,300 in the first quarter of 2023 to 2.8 million in the same quarter in 2026.
In a report, to be published on Wednesday, the commission says crashes have increased significantly in the past five years. They doubled from 209 in the last quarter of 2024 to 405 in the last quarter of 2025, it says.
"This reflects both a rapid increase in use of these devices but is also likely the result of different ridership relative to traditional bicycles, including new riders, food delivery workers, and share schemes," it says.
But the report found mandatory insurance would "introduce new harms" causing some users to stop riding or evade the requirements while others would be left paying disproportionately more than the risk they create.
The report says that while cycling accidents peak in morning and afternoon commuting periods, with bicycles most often involved, "at night and in the early morning e-bike crashes were far more common than normal bicycle crashes".
"The time of day crashes occur indicates that e-bikes might be used in riskier settings than normal bicycles," it says, including "people using e-bikes as an alternative to driving or public transport after a night out".
Achterstraat told The Australian Financial Review the public was concerned "mainly with illegality - both of the machine itself and the behaviour of riders". He noted higher e-bike crash rates in the 9pm to 3am window and said these were less likely to be last-mile trips to help use other transport.
"If there's any skylarking - we've got to stop that. If there are behavioural issues: people getting a bit risky ... going a bit too fast, not wearing a helmet, pushing the envelope. If it's illegal - you just should not do it." Achterstraat recommended greater education and enforcement of existing laws, which would cost $19 million but reap an estimated $74 million productivity gain, a $55 million net improvement.
Transport Minister John Graham said the government accepted the recommendation not to introduce compulsory insurance.
"The report finds that a mandatory insurance scheme for pedal-assisted e-bikes would be too expensive, too difficult to enforce, have limited impact on unsafe behaviour and also deter e-bike use," Graham said.
"As the commissioner says, our primary safety focus should be stopping accidents before they happen and that's exactly what we're doing by reducing power limits, giving police new powers to seize and crush illegal high-powered e-bikes and introducing an age limit."
